lessons.title: Tokens: teaching a computer to read

blocks.html:
A language model never sees your words. It sees a list of integers. Everything it knows, every answer it gives, and every bill you pay for it is counted in those integers, which are called tokens. This chapter shows exactly where they come from. By the end you will have built the same kind of tokenizer GPT-4 uses, trained it on Shakespeare, and measured it against OpenAI's real ones.

Why this matters

Tokenization looks like boring plumbing, and that is why it causes so much confusion. A surprising number of "the model is dumb" moments are really tokenizer moments. Karpathy opens his tokenizer lecture with a list of them: models that struggle to spell, that are worse at arithmetic than they should be, that handle Python indentation badly, that do worse in Polish or Korean than in English, and that warn you about a trailing space in your prompt. Each one traces back to how text was chopped into tokens before the model ever saw it.

You will meet tokens in three places in your work.

First, cost and limits. API prices are per token, input and output. Context windows are measured in tokens. When an agent reads a long file, calls tools, and keeps a conversation history, all of that is tokens, and it is the main thing you pay for and the main thing that runs out. If you can estimate tokens in your head, you can estimate cost and you can tell when an agent is about to forget its own instructions.

Second, model behavior. The model predicts the next token, not the next letter or word. When you understand what the tokens are, a lot of odd behavior becomes predictable instead of mysterious. A model asked how many letters are in a word is being asked about something it mostly cannot see directly.

Third, security. The text a filter inspects and the token sequence a model consumes are two different views of the same input. Rare or strange tokens can make models behave erratically, and the gap between "string the guardrail checked" and "tokens the model reacted to" is one of the places red teamers look. You do not need that today, but you will in the AI Security course, and it starts here.

The idea in plain words

A tokenizer is a translator between text and a list of integers. It has a fixed vocabulary, a big lookup table where every entry is a piece of text with an ID number. To encode, you cut the text into pieces from the vocabulary and write down their IDs. To decode, you look the IDs up and glue the pieces back together. The model only ever works with the IDs.

The whole design question is what the pieces should be.

One option is single characters. The sentence "To be, or not" becomes 13 tokens, one per character. The vocabulary is tiny, so it is easy, but the sequences get long. A model has a fixed context window, so long sequences mean it sees less text at once, and every extra token costs compute.

Another option is whole words. Now "To be, or not" is about five tokens, which is great, until someone types a word that is not in the table: a typo, a new product name, a Polish word, a variable name in code. The model has no ID for it. Word vocabularies also explode, since "run", "runs", "running" and "runner" all need separate entries.

Byte-pair encoding, or BPE, is the compromise almost everyone uses. You start with the smallest possible pieces, the 256 possible byte values, so any text in any language can always be encoded. Then you look at a big pile of training text, find the pair of neighboring pieces that appears most often, and glue that pair into a new piece with a new ID. Repeat that thousands of times. Common things like " the" and " and" end up as single tokens. Rare things still work, they just get split into smaller pieces.

Here is a concrete example from the lab. Training on the first 200,000 characters of Shakespeare, the very first merge BPE chooses is a space followed by the letter t, which appears 4,336 times. The second merge is "h" plus "e", which appears 3,484 times. The ninth merge glues the two earlier results together: " t" plus "he" becomes " the". After 768 merges, the sentence "To be, or not to be, that is the question." comes out as 15 tokens: "To", " be", ",", " or", " not", " to", " be", ",", " that", " is", " the", " qu", "est", "ion", ".". Common words are whole. The rarer word "question" is built from three pieces.

How it actually works

There are four layers, and it helps to keep them separate in your head.

Layer 1: characters become Unicode code points

A Python string is a sequence of Unicode code points. Each character has a number. "H" is 72, "i" is 105, a space is 32, and the Polish letter "ń" is 324. There are well over a hundred thousand code points defined, and the standard keeps growing, so using code points directly as tokens would give you a huge and unstable vocabulary.

Layer 2: code points become UTF-8 bytes

UTF-8 is the standard way to store code points as bytes. Plain English letters take one byte each. Many accented letters take two. Most Chinese, Japanese and Korean characters take three, and emoji take four. In the lab, "Hi ń" is four characters but five bytes: 72, 105, 32, 197, 132. The "ń" needs the pair 197, 132.

Bytes are attractive because there are exactly 256 of them. If your base vocabulary is the 256 bytes, there is no such thing as an unknown character. Anything a computer can store as text can be encoded. This is called byte-level BPE, and it is what GPT-2 introduced for OpenAI's models.

Layer 3: pre-splitting with a regular expression

Before any merging happens, real tokenizers chop text into chunks with a regular expression, and merges are only allowed inside a chunk. The chunks are roughly: a word with an optional leading space, a run of up to three digits, a run of punctuation, and runs of whitespace.

Why bother? Without it, BPE would happily learn tokens like "dog." or "e, t" because those byte pairs happen to be frequent in the training text. You would waste vocabulary on accidents of punctuation, and the same word would get different tokens depending on what followed it. The pre-split keeps word pieces clean. You can see one consequence in the token lists: almost every word token includes its leading space, as in " the" and " be". The space belongs to the word that follows it.

The pattern our library uses is the one from OpenAI's GPT-4 tokenizer, published in the tiktoken source. The library's test suite checks that our regex chunks a tricky sample exactly the way tiktoken's does.

Layer 4: byte-pair merges

Training works like this:

  1. Split the training text into chunks with the regex, and turn each chunk into a list of byte IDs from 0 to 255.
  2. Count every pair of neighbors across all chunks.
  3. Take the most frequent pair, say (32, 116), which is space then "t". Give it the next free ID, 256.
  4. Replace every occurrence of that pair with 256.
  5. Repeat until the vocabulary reaches the size you want.

Each merge makes the text a little shorter. The list of merges, in the order they were learned, is the tokenizer. Nothing else needs to be saved.

Encoding new text replays the merges. For each chunk, start from bytes, look at all neighbor pairs, and apply whichever pair was learned earliest. Repeat until no learned pair is present. Using the learned order matters: it guarantees the encoder reproduces the same decisions training made. tiktoken calls this order the merge rank.

Decoding is the easy direction. Every token ID maps to a fixed string of bytes. Concatenate the bytes and decode them as UTF-8.

Measuring a tokenizer

The useful number is compression, how many bytes of text each token covers on text the tokenizer has not seen. In the lab, on 20,000 bytes of held-out Shakespeare:

  • Raw bytes, vocabulary 256: 1.00 bytes per token, by definition.
  • Our BPE with 512 entries: 1.92.
  • Our BPE with 1,024 entries: 2.31.
  • GPT-2, vocabulary 50,257: 3.07.
  • GPT-4's cl100k_base, about 100,000 entries: 3.49.
  • GPT-4o's o200k_base, about 200,000 entries: 3.57.

Two lessons come out of those numbers. More vocabulary buys more compression, and the returns shrink. Going from 256 to 512 entries almost doubled compression. Going from 100,000 to 200,000 gained about two percent on this English text. The large modern vocabularies are mostly buying better coverage of other languages and of code, which you will see in a moment.

Why the vocabulary size is a real tradeoff

If more vocabulary means shorter sequences, why not use a million tokens? Because the vocabulary is not free inside the model. Each token ID needs an embedding, a learned vector, at the input, and the output layer has to produce a score for every token at every step. In GPT-2 small, the embedding table alone is 50,257 rows of 768 numbers, about 38.6 million parameters, close to a third of the 124 million total. Rare tokens are also a problem: if a token almost never appears in the training data, its embedding barely gets trained. So vocabulary size is a design choice that trades sequence length against model size and token quality. Most frontier labs currently land somewhere between about 100,000 and 260,000 entries.

The four surprises in the lab output

The lab runs the same strings through three of OpenAI's production tokenizers. Each result explains a behavior you have probably seen.

Spelling. In all three tokenizers, " strawberry" with a leading space is a single token. Without the space, it is three: "st", "raw", "berry". When you ask a model how many letter r's are in strawberry, the model is looking at one or three opaque IDs, not ten letters. It has to have learned, from training data, what letters are inside each token. Modern models often get this right now, partly through training and partly by reasoning step by step, but the difficulty comes from here.

Languages. "Good morning, how are you?" is 7 tokens in all three tokenizers. The Polish equivalent, "Dzień dobry, jak się masz?", is 16 tokens in GPT-2, 11 in cl100k and 10 in o200k. In GPT-2, "ń" and "ę" are not even whole tokens; each one is two raw bytes, which is why the decoded pieces show replacement characters. Same meaning, up to more than twice the price and twice the context used. Newer vocabularies spent their extra entries largely on non-English text, and the gap shrinks, but it does not close.

Numbers. GPT-2 tokenizes "127 + 4 = 131" as "127", " +", " 4", " =", " 131". The GPT-4 era tokenizers split digits into runs of at most three and keep the space separate, so 4 becomes " " and "4". That is a deliberate choice to make numbers more consistent, since a number's tokens no longer depend on whether a space came before it. Even so, a model doing arithmetic is operating on chunks like "131", not on digits, which is part of why long arithmetic without tools is unreliable.

Code. Eight spaces of Python indentation followed by "return y" is 9 tokens in GPT-2, because each space is its own token, and 3 tokens in GPT-4's tokenizer, which has tokens for runs of spaces. Karpathy points out that this change made Python denser, so the same context window holds more code. It is one concrete reason GPT-4 got better at code.

Build it

The lab is lab.py in this chapter's folder. The tokenizer code lives in the shared library at labs/tutorlab/tokenizers.py, so later chapters can reuse it, and it is covered by tests in labs/tests/. Run the lab with:

blocks.html:
It runs offline in a few seconds. Here are the important pieces.

Counting pairs and merging

This walks the list once. Whenever it sees the target pair it writes the new ID and skips two places, otherwise it copies one ID and moves on. Note that it scans left to right, so in a run like "aaa" with pair (a, a) it produces the new token followed by a single "a". That is the standard behavior.

Training

Three details are worth noticing. The regex split happens first, so pairs never cross chunk boundaries. Each distinct chunk is processed once and weighted by how often it occurs, which gives the same answer as processing every occurrence, only much faster, since " the" may appear thousands of times. And ties are broken by the smaller pair, so training is deterministic and you get the same tokenizer every run.

The new token's bytes are just the bytes of its two parents glued together. That is why decoding is trivial.

Encoding with merge ranks

Among the pairs present, pick the one with the smallest merge ID, which is the one learned earliest. If none of the pairs was ever learned, the chunk is fully encoded. This is the same rule tiktoken uses with its ranks.

What the lab checks

The check() function at the bottom asserts real behavior, not trivia:

  • Decoding the encoding gives back exactly the original text, including Polish and an emoji the tokenizer never saw in training.
  • The 1,024 entry tokenizer beats 2 bytes per token on unseen text, and compression rises at every step of the vocabulary sweep, starting from exactly 1.00 for raw bytes.
  • The first merge is the most frequent pair.
  • No learned token contains a space in its middle, which proves the regex pre-split is doing its job.
  • The production facts this chapter relies on are true on your machine: GPT-2 has 50,257 tokens, " strawberry" is one token and "strawberry" is three in o200k, Polish costs more in GPT-2 than in o200k, and all three production tokenizers compress better than ours.

If any of those fail, the lab stops with an error instead of printing CHECK PASSED.

Expected output (abridged)

Part 3: training BPE (first 12 merges shown)
  merge   1:     b' ' + b't'     -> b' t'        seen 4,336x
  merge   2:     b'h' + b'e'     -> b'he'        seen 3,484x
  merge   9:    b' t' + b'he'    -> b' the'      seen 1,783x
  ... 768 merges, final vocabulary 1024

Part 4: encode and decode
  pieces ['To', ' be', ',', ' or', ' not', ' to', ' be', ',', ' that', ' is', ' the', ' qu', 'est', 'ion', '.']
  held-out text: 20,000 bytes -> 8,641 tokens = 2.31 bytes per token

Part 5: production tokenizers (tiktoken)
  gpt2         vocabulary  50,257   held-out Shakespeare 3.07 bytes per token
  cl100k_base  vocabulary 100,277   held-out Shakespeare 3.49 bytes per token
  o200k_base   vocabulary 200,019   held-out Shakespeare 3.57 bytes per token

Part 6: same meaning, different price
  gpt2         English 7 tokens, Polish 16 tokens
  o200k_base   English 7 tokens, Polish 10 tokens

CHECK PASSED

blocks.html:
Try this

The bottom of the lab has three experiments. Predict the answer before you run each one, and write the prediction down. The point is to find out whether your mental model is right.

  1. Add 2,048 to the vocabulary sweep. Will the gain from 1,024 to 2,048 be bigger or smaller than the gain from 512 to 1,024?
  2. Train on TEXT.upper(). What happens to "To be, or not" afterwards, and why?
  3. Add a sentence in Polish or German to the samples. Which production tokenizer is cheapest for it?

Common mistakes and misconceptions

"A token is a word." Sometimes it is, often it is not. In the lab, "question" is three tokens, " strawberry" is one, and a single Polish letter can be two. The usable rule of thumb is a measurement, not a definition: on our English text, GPT-4o's tokenizer averaged about 3.6 bytes per token. Code, numbers and other languages differ, so count instead of guessing when it matters.

"The model reads letters." It reads token IDs. Whatever it knows about the letters inside a token, it had to learn from data. That is why spelling, counting characters, reversing strings and rhyming can be harder than they look, and why asking the model to spell a word out first often helps: spelling it out turns letters into separate tokens it can see.

"The tokenizer is learned along with the model." It is trained separately, before the model, on its own data, and then frozen. The model's training never changes it. You can swap in a different tokenizer only by retraining or heavily adapting the model, because every embedding row is tied to a specific token ID.

"Bigger vocabulary is always better." Bigger vocabularies shorten sequences, but they grow the embedding and output layers and leave rare tokens undertrained. The returns also shrink, as the sweep and the 100,000 versus 200,000 comparison show.

"Token counts are the same across models." They are not. The same Polish sentence was 16, 11 and 10 tokens in three OpenAI tokenizers, and other vendors use other tokenizers again. Budget and price per model, using that model's own counter.

"Glitch tokens are a myth." They were real. Researchers found tokens such as " SolidGoldMagikarp" in the GPT-2 and GPT-3 vocabulary that appeared in the tokenizer's training data but almost never in the model's, so the model never learned what to do with them, and asking about them produced bizarre output. Karpathy covers this in the lecture linked below.

In the real world

OpenAI ships its tokenizers as the open source tiktoken library. As of tiktoken 0.14.0 (checked October 10, 2026), its model table maps GPT-2 to the "gpt2" encoding, GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 Turbo to "cl100k_base", and GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, o1 and GPT-5 to "o200k_base". You can see that table in the tiktoken source on GitHub. tiktoken does exactly what our code does, regex pre-split followed by rank-ordered byte-pair merges, but it is written in Rust and is far faster.

Meta's Llama 3 moved to a 128,000 token vocabulary, which Meta's launch post says "encodes language much more efficiently". Llama 2 had used a 32,000 entry BPE vocabulary built with Google's SentencePiece library, according to the Llama 2 paper. SentencePiece is another popular implementation that works on Unicode text directly and can fall back to bytes for rare characters.

Anthropic does not publish a downloadable tokenizer for its current Claude models. Instead it provides a token counting endpoint in the API, so you can ask how many tokens a message will use before you send it. As of October 2026 that is the reliable way to count Claude tokens.

In agent tools like Claude Code, Codex and Hermes, token counts drive everything you care about operationally: when the context gets compacted, how much a long session costs, and how much of a big file the model can actually read. When an agent "forgets" something from earlier, the cause is usually that the conversation crossed a token limit and was summarized or truncated.

To explore tokenizers interactively, the Tiktokenizer web app shows how any text splits under several real tokenizers. Karpathy uses it throughout his lecture.

Go deeper

Watch these after you have run the lab. They will make much more sense once you have trained your own tokenizer.

  • Andrej Karpathy, "Let's build the GPT Tokenizer". This is the full version of this chapter, over two hours, building minbpe live.
  • Start at 4:49 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zduSFxRajkE&t=289) for his list of model failures caused by tokenization, including spelling, then keep going through 5:27 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zduSFxRajkE&t=327) for SolidGoldMagikarp.
  • Jump to 22:30 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zduSFxRajkE&t=1350) for byte-pair encoding itself, where he builds the merge loop step by step.
  • 68:20 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zduSFxRajkE&t=4100) walks through the GPT-4 regex pattern, including the whitespace rule that made Python denser.
  • Andrej Karpathy, "Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT". At 12:04 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7xTGNNLPyMI&t=724) he introduces tokenization as part of the whole pipeline and shows GPT-4's tokenizer on screen. Good for seeing where tokens sit in the bigger picture before the next chapters.
  • Papers and code: the GPT-2 paper (section 2.2 explains byte-level BPE), Sennrich and colleagues' 2015 paper that brought BPE to neural machine translation, Karpathy's minbpe repository, and the SolidGoldMagikarp write-up on LessWrong. All are linked in Sources.

Explain it back

Without looking at this page, explain to someone who has never written code why a model can know what a strawberry is but still miscount the letter r in it. Use the words token, vocabulary and merge, and mention what the leading space has to do with it. Aim for about a minute. Explain it to a study partner or record your own explanation.

Check yourself

The full check is in quiz.json: four multiple choice questions, two predict-the-output questions, and two explain questions with rubrics. The multiple-choice questions below check recall; the downloadable quiz also includes prediction and explanation rubrics. The questions cover:

  1. Why byte-level BPE can encode any text.
  2. What the regex pre-split prevents.
  3. The order merges are applied in during encoding.
  4. Why vocabulary size is a tradeoff.
  5. Predicting compression when the vocabulary grows.
  6. Predicting the tokens for a number in a GPT-4 era tokenizer.
  7. Explaining the cost gap between English and Polish.
  8. Explaining why spelling is hard for language models.

blocks.source:
"""Lab: Tokens, teaching a computer to read.

Goal: build a real byte-level BPE tokenizer (the GPT-2/GPT-4 design), train it on
Shakespeare, and compare it with OpenAI's production tokenizers.

Run:  python lab.py
Runs offline in about 20 seconds. Everything it needs is in labs/ (Tiny Shakespeare
and a local cache of OpenAI's tiktoken vocabularies).
"""
import os
import pathlib
import sys

LABS = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parents[3] / 'labs'
sys.path.insert(0, str(LABS))
os.environ['TIKTOKEN_CACHE_DIR'] = str(LABS / 'data' / 'tiktoken-cache')   # offline: use the local copy

import tiktoken  # noqa: E402

from tutorlab.tokenizers import BPETokenizer, CharTokenizer  # noqa: E402

TEXT = (LABS / 'data' / 'tinyshakespeare.txt').read_text()
TRAIN = TEXT[:200_000]      # train on the first ~200 KB
HELD_OUT = TEXT[-20_000:]   # measure on text the tokenizer never saw

# --- Part 1: text is already numbers -------------------------------------------
print('Part 1: what a computer actually stores')
word = 'Hi ń'
print(f'  string            {word!r}')
print(f'  Unicode points    {[ord(c) for c in word]}')
print(f'  UTF-8 bytes       {list(word.encode("utf-8"))}   <- "ń" needs 2 bytes')

# --- Part 2: the simplest tokenizer, one token per character -------------------
print('\nPart 2: character tokenizer')
char_tok = CharTokenizer(TEXT)
ids = char_tok.encode('To be, or not')
print(f'  vocabulary size   {char_tok.vocab_size}  (every distinct character in Shakespeare)')
print(f'  "To be, or not" -> {ids}')
print(f'  decoded back    -> {char_tok.decode(ids)!r}')
try:
    char_tok.encode('Dzień')
except ValueError as e:
    print(f'  "Dzień" fails     {e}')

# --- Part 3: train byte-pair encoding ------------------------------------------
print('\nPart 3: training BPE (first 12 merges shown)')
bpe = BPETokenizer()
history = bpe.train(TRAIN, vocab_size=1024)
for (a, b), new_id, n in history[:12]:
    print(f'  merge {new_id - 255:3d}: {bpe.vocab[a]!r:>8} + {bpe.vocab[b]!r:<8} -> {bpe.vocab[new_id]!r:<12} seen {n:,}x')
print(f'  ... {len(history)} merges, final vocabulary {bpe.vocab_size}')
print(f'  a few late tokens: {[bpe.vocab[i].decode("utf-8", "replace") for i in range(1000, 1012)]}')

# --- Part 4: encode, decode, and compression -----------------------------------
print('\nPart 4: encode and decode')
line = 'To be, or not to be, that is the question.'
print(f'  pieces {bpe.tokens(line)}')
print(f'  ids    {bpe.encode(line)}')
n_bytes = len(HELD_OUT.encode('utf-8'))
n_tokens = len(bpe.encode(HELD_OUT))
print(f'  held-out text: {n_bytes:,} bytes -> {n_tokens:,} tokens = {n_bytes / n_tokens:.2f} bytes per token')
print(f'  "Dzień dobry" -> {bpe.tokens("Dzień dobry")}  (no crash: any text is just bytes)')

print('\n  vocabulary size vs compression (same training text, held-out text):')
sweep = {}
for v in (256, 384, 512, 768, 1024):
    t = bpe if v == 1024 else BPETokenizer()
    if v != 1024:
        t.train(TRAIN, vocab_size=v)
    sweep[v] = n_bytes / len(t.encode(HELD_OUT))
    print(f'    vocab {v:5d}  {sweep[v]:.2f} bytes per token  {"#" * round(sweep[v] * 10)}')

# --- Part 5: the real thing, OpenAI's tokenizers -------------------------------
print('\nPart 5: production tokenizers (tiktoken)')
encs = {name: tiktoken.get_encoding(name) for name in ('gpt2', 'cl100k_base', 'o200k_base')}
prod_ratio = {}
for name, enc in encs.items():
    prod_ratio[name] = n_bytes / len(enc.encode(HELD_OUT))
    print(f'  {name:12} vocabulary {enc.n_vocab:7,}   held-out Shakespeare {prod_ratio[name]:.2f} bytes per token')
samples = ['strawberry', ' strawberry', 'Dzień dobry, jak się masz?', '127 + 4 = 131', '        return y']
for s in samples:
    print(f'  {s!r}')
    for name, enc in encs.items():
        pieces = [enc.decode_single_token_bytes(t).decode('utf-8', 'replace') for t in enc.encode(s)]
        print(f'      {name:12} {len(pieces):2d} tokens {pieces}')

print('\nPart 6: same meaning, different price')
en, pl = 'Good morning, how are you?', 'Dzień dobry, jak się masz?'
for name, enc in encs.items():
    print(f'  {name:12} English {len(enc.encode(en))} tokens, Polish {len(enc.encode(pl))} tokens')


# TRY THIS (predict first, then run):
#   1. Add 2048 to the sweep. Will the gain from 1024 to 2048 be bigger or smaller than 512 to 1024? Why?
#   2. Train on TEXT.upper() instead. What happens to "To be, or not" afterwards?
#   3. Add your own sentence in Polish or German to `samples`. Which tokenizer is cheapest?


def check():
    # Round trip must be exact for any text, including unseen Unicode.
    for s in ['To be, or not', 'Dzień dobry 🙂', HELD_OUT[:3000]]:
        assert bpe.decode(bpe.encode(s)) == s, f'round trip failed for {s[:20]!r}'
    # BPE must compress better than one byte per token on unseen English.
    assert n_bytes / n_tokens > 2.0, 'a 1024 vocabulary should beat 2 bytes per token on held-out English'
    # 256 = raw bytes, exactly 1 byte per token; every larger vocabulary compresses more.
    assert abs(sweep[256] - 1.0) < 1e-9
    assert all(sweep[a] < sweep[b] for a, b in zip(sorted(sweep), sorted(sweep)[1:]))
    # The first merge is the most common pair in the training text.
    assert history[0][2] == max(c for _, _, c in history), 'first merge must be the most frequent'
    # Regex pre-split means no learned token straddles a word and punctuation.
    assert all(not (p.strip() and ' ' in p.strip()) for p in (v.decode('utf-8', 'replace') for v in bpe.vocab.values()))
    # Production facts used in the chapter.
    assert encs['gpt2'].n_vocab == 50257
    assert all(r > n_bytes / n_tokens for r in prod_ratio.values()), 'big vocabularies should beat our 1024'
    assert len(encs['o200k_base'].encode(' strawberry')) == 1
    assert len(encs['o200k_base'].encode('strawberry')) == 3
    assert len(encs['gpt2'].encode(pl)) > len(encs['o200k_base'].encode(pl))


check()
print('\nCHECK PASSED')

quiz.q: Why can a byte-level BPE tokenizer encode any text, including a language it never saw in training?
choices: Its vocabulary includes every word in every language
Its base vocabulary is the 256 possible byte values, and all text is stored as bytes
It falls back to an UNK token for unknown characters
It retrains itself on new text automatically
quiz.why: Any UTF-8 text is a sequence of bytes, and all 256 bytes are in the base vocabulary, so the worst case is one token per byte.

quiz.q: What does the regular-expression pre-split prevent?
choices: Merges that cross word, number, punctuation or whitespace boundaries, such as 'dog.'
quiz.why: Merges are only allowed inside a chunk, so vocabulary is not wasted on accidental combinations like a word plus its punctuation.

quiz.q: When encoding new text, which merge does the tokenizer apply next?
choices: The pair that is most frequent in the new text
The pair that produces the longest token
Among pairs present, the one that was learned earliest in training (lowest rank)
quiz.why: Replaying merges in training order reproduces the exact decisions training made. tiktoken calls this order the rank.

quiz.q: Which is a real cost of a much larger vocabulary?
choices: A bigger embedding table and output layer, plus rare tokens that barely get trained
The tokenizer can no longer encode emoji
quiz.why: Each token needs an embedding row and an output score; GPT-2 small spends about 38.6M of its 124M parameters on the embedding table. Rare tokens get few training updates.

quiz.q: In o200k_base, how many tokens is ' strawberry' (with a leading space) versus 'strawberry'?
quiz.why: Measured in the lab: the space-prefixed word is a single token, the bare word splits into 'st', 'raw', 'berry'.

selfCheck.q: The lab's sweep showed 1.92 bytes per token at vocabulary 512 and 2.31 at 1,024. If you train with 2,048, will the gain be larger or smaller than 0.39?
selfCheck.answer: Smaller. With the same 200,000 character training text, a 2,048 vocabulary measured 2.65 bytes per token, a gain of 0.34 versus 0.39 for 512 to 1,024.
selfCheck.why: Each new merge covers a less frequent pair than the one before, so compression rises with diminishing returns.

selfCheck.q: What tokens does cl100k_base produce for '127 + 4 = 131'?
selfCheck.why: The digit rule matches runs of 1 to 3 digits without a leading space, so the space before a number becomes its own token.

selfCheck.q: Explain why the same request costs more in Polish than in English, using the lab's numbers.
rubric: Vocabulary built mostly from English-heavy data has more whole-word tokens for English
Polish letters like ń and ę take two UTF-8 bytes and may not be single tokens
Numbers: English 7 tokens in all three; Polish 16 in GPT-2, 11 in cl100k, 10 in o200k
Price and context use are per token, so more tokens means more cost and less room

selfCheck.q: Explain why a model that knows what a strawberry is can still miscount its r's.
rubric: The model sees token IDs, not letters
' strawberry' is one token; 'strawberry' is three
Letter content of a token must be learned indirectly from data
Spelling the word out first turns letters into separate tokens and helps

lessons.title: Embeddings: giving each token a vector of meaning

blocks.html:
A token ID tells the model which entry you meant. It does not tell the model what to do with that entry. The next step is surprisingly small: keep a table of adjustable numbers and use the ID to select a row. That row is the token's embedding. The interesting part is not the lookup. It is how training changes the table, and what the resulting geometry does and does not mean.

Why this matters

In the previous chapter, you turned text into token IDs. Stop there and you have a useful encoding, but not a useful representation for reasoning about language. The numerical distance between two IDs is arbitrary. If the tokenizer assigns neighboring IDs to unrelated pieces of text, those pieces do not suddenly become similar. A model needs adjustable representations rather than an accidental ordering imposed by its dictionary.

Embeddings solve that problem by giving the model parameters associated with each token. Downstream calculations can multiply, add and compare these parameters. Training can change them when doing so improves an objective. This is the bridge from discrete symbols to a differentiable model: the IDs stay discrete while the numbers selected by those IDs can be adjusted continuously.

You will meet this bridge while reading model code, debugging tensor shapes, sizing a local model, or building retrieval for an agent. The word embedding appears in all those settings, but it does not always name the same object. A token lookup inside a language model is not automatically a sentence representation suitable for document search. Being able to distinguish them prevents a plausible-looking demo from becoming an unreliable application.

There is also a useful defensive engineering lesson. A high similarity score is not proof that a retrieved passage is true, authorized, or safe to treat as instructions. Similarity is an ordering rule produced by a representation and a metric. An agent still needs source checks and permission boundaries outside that ordering rule. We will not build a security system here. We will build enough understanding to avoid confusing a numerical resemblance with a trust decision.

This chapter extends the Academy's random-table demonstration with a hand calculation, a gradient trace, an actual supervised training experiment, and tests that can catch a wrong explanation. The training data is deliberately synthetic. That limitation is part of the lesson, not something to hide behind a polished cosine score.

The idea in plain words

Imagine a labeled drawer for every token. Inside each drawer is a short list of numbers. Asking for a token retrieves the numbers from its drawer. No multiplication of the token ID is involved, and no dictionary definition is stored there in plain English.

The lab uses the vocabulary cat, dog, run, walk, the, and a. Each entry has a row of four floating-point numbers. With the lab's seeded random initialization, the row for cat, rounded for display, is [1.927, 1.487, 0.901, -2.106]. These numbers are not a finding about cats. They are a random starting point. The phrase the cat run becomes IDs [4, 0, 2], then an array with shape (3, 4): a row for each token occurrence, with four coordinates per row.

That short list is a vector. The full collection of rows is a matrix. The lookup table is called an embedding layer because it places discrete token identities into a space where numerical operations are possible. In PyTorch, nn.Embedding is exactly this kind of learnable lookup table, as its official documentation makes explicit.

To make the vectors useful, we need a task. In the lab's small supervised experiment, the task is to reproduce supplied context-frequency patterns. The supplied pattern for cat resembles the one for dog; the patterns for run and walk resemble each other instead. Training moves the corresponding rows toward those patterns. We can then measure which rows point in similar directions.

The careful version of “a vector of meaning” is therefore: a vector of learned numbers that is useful for a particular objective. It may encode useful linguistic regularities. It is not a universal meaning barcode, and a randomly initialized vector has not learned any linguistic regularities at all.

How it actually works

Part 1: select a row, preserve the surrounding shape

Call the embedding table E. Let V be the vocabulary size and D the embedding width. E has shape V by D. A token ID i is an integer used as a row address. Its embedding is E[i], a vector containing D numbers. The table has V times D adjustable entries, irrespective of how many tokens happen to appear in the current input.

Our table has shape (6, 4) and contains 24 parameters. Looking up a sequence of shape (3,) returns (3, 4). Looking up a batch of shape (2, 3) returns (2, 3, 4). The batch dimension counts examples, the sequence dimension counts token positions, and the last dimension contains the coordinates attached to each occurrence. PyTorch's shape rule is to append the embedding width to the input shape.

Repeated occurrences share the same underlying row. If cat appears again, the lookup returns the same values again, provided the table has not changed. This is parameter sharing, not copying independent parameters into every position. During training, feedback from all those occurrences can flow back into the shared row.

There is another way to express the same operation. Make a vector with a single one at the token's index and zeros elsewhere. This is a one-hot vector. Multiplying that vector by E selects the corresponding row, because every other row is multiplied by zero. For a sequence, stack the one-hot vectors and perform a matrix multiplication. The lab checks that this equals direct lookup exactly.

That equivalence explains the math; it is not a reason to allocate a huge one-hot array in production. Direct indexing gets the same result without explicitly storing all those zeros. The ID is an address, the one-hot vector is an optional mathematical description of that address, and the embedding is the floating-point row selected by it.

Part 2: compare directions without confusing them with lengths

A dot product multiplies matching coordinates and adds the products. For vectors u and v, written as lists of coordinates, the dot product is the sum of u[j] times v[j] over coordinate index j. A norm is a vector's length. The Euclidean norm is the square root of the sum of its squared coordinates.

Cosine similarity divides the dot product by the product of the lengths:

blocks.source: cosine(u, v) = dot(u, v) / (norm(u) * norm(v))

blocks.html:
Here dot combines matching coordinates, norm measures length, and the denominator removes the effect of positive rescaling. For nonzero vectors, the result measures directional alignment. It is the cosine of the angle, not the angle itself. Same direction gives one, perpendicular directions give zero, and opposite directions give minus one. These are geometric statements, not automatic claims about synonyms or antonyms.

Work through the lab's vectors u = [3, 4] and v = [4, 3]. Multiply each matching pair and add to obtain a dot product of 24. Each vector has length 5. Divide 24 by the product of those lengths to obtain 0.960. The lab performs this arithmetic directly and checks it against torch.nn.functional.cosine_similarity.

Now compare u with a positively scaled copy of itself. The lab multiplies u by 2 and gets cosine 1.000, although the dot product is now 50.0. The direction stayed the same while the length changed. This is why a dot-product ranking and a cosine ranking can disagree if the candidate vectors have different lengths. Normalizing both the query and every candidate to unit length makes their dot products equal their cosines.

There is an important exception: the zero vector has no direction. The mathematical expression divides by zero. Our helper rejects such a row. PyTorch's cosine function instead uses a small epsilon in the denominator for numerical stability, and returns 0.0 for the lab's zero-vector comparison. That software convention does not give the zero vector a geometric angle. If zeros represent padding or missing data, handle that meaning deliberately rather than accepting a score without inspection.

The same caution applies to a token compared with itself. Any ordinary nonzero vector has self-cosine one, including an untrained random vector. Self-similarity is a useful arithmetic check, but it cannot establish that a model learned language. Our lab proves that the self-similarity check passes before any training has happened.

Part 3: discover where learning enters the lookup

A table looks static, so how can it learn? The floating-point entries can participate in calculations whose result is a loss, a number measuring how badly a task was performed. Differentiation tells us how changing each entry would change that loss. That sensitivity is called its gradient. A training update changes parameters in a direction intended to reduce the loss.

The lookup index is not what we differentiate. We differentiate the selected numbers. If an output depends on a particular row, its gradient contribution goes back to that row. Contributions from repeated occurrences add together because they refer to the same parameter.

The lab isolates this mechanism without a language model. It looks up IDs [0, 0, 1] and sums every selected entry. Every selected coordinate contributes directly to that sum. The gradient on every cat coordinate is 2.0 because that row appeared twice. Every dog coordinate has gradient 1.0. The other rows have zero gradient from this calculation because none of their entries contributed to the sum.

This sum is a teaching probe, not a useful language objective. It makes the routing of gradients obvious. Do not generalize the zero-gradient observation to all optimizers and architectures. Weight decay can affect parameters separately from this lookup, accumulated optimizer state can matter, and a tied output layer can supply another gradient path. What we have proved is narrower: the plain lookup's backward pass accumulates contributions into selected rows.

Part 4: make a small table actually learn

To expose the entire learning mechanism, we supervise the embedding directly with a tiny hand-authored context fixture. Its columns are labeled purrs, barks, quickly, and slowly. These are illustrative context labels, not a measured English corpus. The deliberately artificial counts make the relationship between target data and final geometry visible.

The row for cat contains counts [8, 2, 0, 0]. Dividing by the row total produces the target [0.8, 0.2, 0.0, 0.0]. The row for dog produces [0.7, 0.3, 0.0, 0.0]. The motion words put their mass in the other coordinates, while the and a deliberately receive identical targets. The fixture is not claiming that cats literally bark with a measured frequency. We supplied a convenient, artificial pattern to study optimization.

Let T be the target matrix. Our loss L is half the sum of (E[i,j] - T[i,j]) squared over every token index i and coordinate index j. Subtraction measures the error, squaring makes positive and negative errors contribute positively, summing combines all entries, and the factor one half makes the derivative simple. For this particular loss, the gradient of an entry is just its current value minus its target.

The update rule is “new entry equals old entry minus learning rate times gradient.” The learning rate controls the size of the step. Our rate is 0.2, and the loop performs 80 updates. This is plain gradient descent written out directly, not an unexplained optimizer call.

The lab prints a worked coordinate. Its starting weight is 1.926915, the target is 0.800000, the gradient is 1.126915, and the next value is 1.701532. These displayed values are rounded from the executed calculation. Read the update literally: the weight is too large, its gradient is positive, and subtracting a positive correction moves it toward the target.

After training, the maximum absolute target error is 0.000000119. The cosine between cat and dog is 0.987241, while cat and run print 0.000000 at the displayed precision. The rows for the and a have cosine 1.000000 because their supplied targets match. The nearest-other-row lookup now pairs the motion words together and pairs the articles together.

Do not conclude that we discovered language from scratch. We fitted explicit targets that we designed to have those relationships. There is no held-out language evaluation. Real language models learn embeddings through a prediction objective coupled to other layers; they are not usually given these named target coordinates. Mikolov and colleagues' work on learned word representations is a historical entry point to that broader idea. Our narrow experiment proves that a loss can train lookup parameters and thereby change measurable geometry.

Part 5: separate geometry from arbitrary labels

If IDs are only addresses, changing every address consistently should preserve the result. The lab permutes the rows and applies the corresponding inverse mapping to the IDs. Every token still retrieves its original vector. Changing just the IDs without changing the table would instead select the wrong rows. This is why a tokenizer and its model weights form a contract.

Coordinates also need not have fixed human names. The lab rotates every learned vector with the same orthogonal matrix and verifies that all pairwise cosines remain unchanged. An orthogonal transformation preserves lengths and dot products, even though individual coordinate values change. This is a geometric demonstration, not a claim that you can rotate one layer of a complete model without adapting the rest of the model.

In our supervised fixture the coordinates have names because we imposed those names in T. Ordinary learned latent coordinates are not generally a tidy list such as “animalness, speed, politeness.” Useful properties may be distributed across coordinates. Avoid reading a single negative number as negative sentiment or a single large coordinate as proof of a specific concept.

Build it

Run from the project root:

blocks.source: env -u PYTHONPATH .venv/bin/python chapters/llm-fundamentals/02-embeddings/lab.py

blocks.html:
The lab adds the shared labs/ directory to its Python import path using its own file location. It therefore also works when invoked by absolute path from another directory. It uses the CPU, needs no API keys or network access, and does not download a model. The reusable helpers live in labs/tutorlab/embeddings_demo.py; their tests live in labs/tests/test_embeddings_demo.py.

Start with Part 1 rather than jumping to the learned scores. torch.manual_seed makes the random initialization reproducible in the tested environment. nn.Embedding creates the table. The STOI dictionary maps our visible token strings to integer row addresses. Passing dtype=torch.long constructs integer indices, rather than floating values that might mistakenly be interpreted as data coordinates.

blocks.source:
ids = torch.tensor([STOI[t] for t in ['the', 'cat', 'run']], dtype=torch.long)
vectors = table(ids)
one_hot = F.one_hot(ids, num_classes=len(VOCAB)).to(table.weight.dtype)

blocks.html:
The final conversion changes the one-hot tensor to the table's floating-point type before multiplication. It does not turn the token IDs into meanings. Compare the direct result with one_hot @ table.weight; the equality check verifies the row-selection explanation.

Our small string wrapper rejects an unknown token rather than inventing a vector. This is not a replacement for the previous chapter's byte-level tokenizer. That tokenizer can split unfamiliar text into known pieces. Our fixture has a deliberately closed vocabulary so that row addresses remain easy to inspect.

In Part 2, cosine_matrix divides each row by its own length and multiplies the resulting matrix by its transpose. The result contains all pairwise cosines. The helper checks shape, floating type, finite values, and nonzero row lengths first. Those checks prevent an invalid input from quietly looking like a meaningful ranking.

In Part 3, .backward() populates the table's .grad tensor. In Part 4, the training loop first clears old gradients because PyTorch accumulates them by default. It then computes the loss, differentiates, and changes the weights inside torch.no_grad(). That context says not to build another differentiation graph for the parameter-update operation itself. detach().clone() preserves the original numbers for a genuine before-and-after comparison rather than retaining a view of changing weights.

blocks.source:
loss = 0.5 * (table(ids) - targets).square().sum()
table.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
loss.backward()
with torch.no_grad():
    table.weight -= lr * table.weight.grad

blocks.html:
The full loop evaluates once more after the last update so the final reported loss belongs to the final table. Its random-number context also restores the caller's random state afterward. That small library courtesy prevents this teaching experiment from unexpectedly changing later seeded experiments.

These excerpts are copied from the executed build/lab-output.txt:

blocks.source:
ids [4, 0, 2] -> shape (3, 4)
  batch shape (2, 3, 4); table parameters 24
  lookup equals one_hot @ weight: True
  self cosine is one even before training: True
  step  0 half-squared-error sum=14.9425401688
  step  1 half-squared-error sum=9.5632257462
  step 10 half-squared-error sum=0.1722757369
  step 40 half-squared-error sum=0.0000002640
  step 80 half-squared-error sum=0.0000000000
  max target error=0.000000119
  trained cosine(cat, dog)=0.987241
  trained cosine(cat, run)=0.000000
  trained cosine(the, a)=1.000000

blocks.html:
The displayed final loss rounds to zero; the separate maximum-error line shows why that is not proof of exact mathematical equality. The code uses tolerances for floating-point checks. It does not replace a failed scientific claim with prettier formatting.

At the end, check() verifies lookup equivalence, shapes, the hand cosine, repeated-index gradients, training convergence, expected neighbors for this fixture, consistent ID relabeling, and rotation invariance. Only then does it print CHECK PASSED. The shared tests also exercise invalid inputs and confirm that a single update matches the analytic update rule.

Try an intervention after predicting its effect. Set the training step count to zero: self-cosine should still pass while the convergence checks fail. Replace the dog's target counts with the run counts: the learned neighborhood should reflect your changed supervision, and assertions tied to the original fixture may fail intentionally. Repeat the cat ID again in the gradient probe: predict which row changes its gradient and which rows do not. Preserve the original gated file when experimenting, so your exercise does not overwrite the verified reference.

Common mistakes and misconceptions

“An embedding layer has already learned meaning when I construct it.” The default table begins randomly initialized. The lab's untrained cat and dog cosine is 0.393828, but that is not a calibrated semantic statement. Even a plausible nearest neighbor can occur by chance. Training evidence must refer to an objective and to observations beyond a self-similarity check.

“Cosine is a probability that two texts mean the same thing.” It is a normalized dot product. It can be negative, and its relationship to task relevance depends on the model and training data. A threshold needs evaluation on the actual retrieval task. Our cat and dog score does not tell you how often a document search would be correct.

“Opposite meanings must point in opposite directions.” Geometry does not enforce that. Opposing words can occur in similar grammatical and topical contexts. What a learned representation considers close depends on what training rewarded, not on a rule that dictionary antonyms must have negative cosine.

“One dimension has one permanent English meaning.” Our named coordinates are an intentionally supervised special case. The rotation experiment preserves the similarities while changing coordinates. A nice visual axis label is an explanatory aid, not evidence that a production model learned exactly that axis.

“Every occurrence gets its own independent parameters.” Occurrences of the same token share a table row. Contextual representations arise later when the model combines the lookup with position information and surrounding text. The static lookup does not by itself know which sentence supplied the token.

“Nearest means trustworthy.” A search returns the highest-scoring available candidate even if every candidate is unsuitable. It can return the query itself unless you exclude that row. Our helper explicitly masks self-matches. Production retrieval also needs relevance evaluation and source handling; a numerical ranking cannot decide authority.

In the real world

The following implementation references were checked as of 2026-10-10. They describe the linked code and documentation, not undisclosed internals of a current proprietary model.

PyTorch documents nn.Embedding as a learnable lookup table and specifies that the embedding width is appended to the input shape. Its padding_idx option suppresses the lookup gradient for a designated padding row. Its from_pretrained convenience constructor defaults to frozen weights. If you expect a supplied table to learn, inspect whether gradients are enabled rather than assuming the word pretrained implies fine-tuning.

Karpathy's nanoGPT defines token embeddings with nn.Embedding(config.vocab_size, config.n_embd) and position embeddings with a separate table. The local labs/tutorlab/gpt.py uses the same overall arrangement. Its forward pass adds token and position embeddings, then passes the result through transformer blocks. That is the concrete boundary between this chapter's static lookup and the later context-dependent computation.

The local GPT implementation also ties its output projection weights to its token embedding weights. The same parameter table can then participate both in input lookup and in output scoring. This is why the gradient caveat above matters: “the token was absent from input” does not by itself imply that its shared row receives no training signal anywhere in the network.

Table size is real memory. The lab calculates a hypothetical vocabulary of 50,000 entries and width 768, giving 38,400,000 parameters. At float32, those weights alone require 153,600,000 bytes, or 153.6 decimal MB. This is an illustrative configuration, not a claimed parameter count for a named deployed model. Training also needs memory for gradients, optimizer state when applicable, activations, and other layers. Lookup output size depends on batch and sequence length; table size does not.

For document retrieval, Sentence Transformers documents encoding complete texts and comparing their resulting embeddings. Those representations come from a text-encoding model, not from looking up an arbitrary single token row. Using the same vector width does not make different models' coordinate systems interchangeable. Keep the query and document encoding procedure compatible, and evaluate on actual relevance judgments rather than borrowing a cosine threshold from an unrelated system.

Go deeper

The lecture moments in lectures.json were verified using the supplied lookup tool on 2026-10-10. YouTube blocked transcript access from this host, so verification used creator-published chapter markers. The anchor phrases below are marker titles, not claimed verbatim spoken quotations.

  • Andrej Karpathy, Building makemore Part 2: MLP, 65:27, marker “visualizing the character embeddings.” Compare learned character geometry with our explicitly named context targets. Ask which properties came from the training task rather than from an axis label supplied by the teacher.
  • 3Blue1Brown, Transformers, the tech behind LLMs, 12:27, marker “Word embeddings.” Use the spatial visualization to build intuition for vectors and directions. Remember that a drawn low-dimensional picture is not the full high-dimensional table.
  • Continue at 18:25, marker “Embeddings beyond words,” to connect a token's initial vector with representations that depend on surrounding text. Attention is a later chapter; you only need to recognize what the lookup alone cannot do.

Read the PyTorch Embedding page alongside Part 1, then its cosine function documentation alongside Part 2. For historical context, Mikolov and colleagues' paper studies representations learned from large datasets and evaluated for syntactic and semantic similarity. Contrast that evidence with our intentionally limited target-fitting exercise. The gap is useful: it separates proving a mechanism from proving broad language ability.

Explain it back

Explain to someone who understands dictionaries but not neural networks how a token ID becomes a useful vector. Use the lab's row lookup and repeated-token gradient as your concrete example. Finish by explaining why self-cosine one does not establish learning and why our successful fixture fit does not establish language understanding. Dictation is fine. Your study partner will check one gap at a time, then ask you to apply the explanation to a changed target pattern before recording mastery.

Check yourself

The questions and answer rubrics are in quiz.json. Answers stay there so you can predict before checking. Reading this chapter or receiving its video is not mastery evidence.

  1. What does an embedding lookup actually do with a token ID?
  2. What shape does a batched lookup return, and why?
  3. What does cosine preserve when a vector is positively rescaled?
  4. Why is self-similarity not proof of learning?
  5. Which relationship does this synthetic training experiment establish, and which claim does it not establish?
  6. Predict the repeated-ID gradient in the sum probe.
  7. Predict what remains valid if the training loop makes no updates.
  8. Explain how token IDs can be relabeled without changing the vectors retrieved.
  9. Explain the difference between a static token embedding and a document representation used for retrieval.
  10. Apply the learning mechanism to a changed context target rather than memorizing the current nearest neighbors.
